title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 830–832 (Night 182, continuing nights-181), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 182 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Dahnash, delighted by Maymūna's ode, answers with an ode of his own in praise of Budūr, followed by a poem by another poet. Each ifrit insists that their own beloved is the lovelier, until Maymūna shrieks at him and Dahnash backs down and proposes a judge. Maymūna strikes the ground, and up comes Qashqash, a one-eyed, hunchbacked, mangy ifrit with seven horns and hooves like a wild ass. He gazes at the sleeping pair, recites verses on two lovers on one bed, and rules that they are equal in beauty; to settle it, he proposes waking one of them without the other's knowing, and whichever burns more for the other is the lesser. Dahnash turns himself into a flea and bites Qamar al-Zamān, who starts up from sleep. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-second night,
sentences.n: al-thāniya, “the second”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ دَهْنَشَ لَمَّا سَمِعَ شِعْرَ مَيْمُونَةَ اهْتَزَّ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الطَّرَبِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu-anna al-ʿifrīta Dahnasha lammā samiʿa shiʿra Maymūnata ihtazza min shiddati al-ṭarabi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-ifrit Dahnash, when he-heard (the) poetry (of) Maymūna, shook from (the) intensity (of) the-delight.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the ifrit Dahnash heard Maymūna's verses, he shook with the force of his delight.
sentences.n: السعيدان is set solid in the print: al-saʿīdu, “fortunate”, and anna, “that”, run together as one word, and it is pointed here across the join. ihtazza, Form VIII of hazza, “to shake”: to quiver, to be stirred. min, “from”, gives the cause: shiddat al-ṭarab, “the intensity of delight”. The shadda of اهتزّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ إِنَّكِ أَنْشَدْتِ فِيمَنْ تَعْشَقِينَهُ وَأَحْسَنْتِ فِي وَصْفِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla innaki anshadti fī-man taʿshaqīnahu wa-aḥsanti fī waṣfihi
sentences.l: And-he-said: Indeed-you(f.) recited about-whom you-love-him, and-you-did-well in describing-him;
sentences.i: and he said, “You have recited verses on the one you love, and described him well;
sentences.n: After qāla, “he said”, inna takes a kasra: innaki, “indeed you” (f.). فيمن, fī-man, is fī, “about”, with man, “whom”, written as one word as it regularly is. taʿshaqīna is the feminine “you love”; its -hu points back to man. aḥsana fī, “to do well at”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا الْآخَرُ لَابُدَّأَنِّي أَبْذُلُ الْجَهْدَ عَلَى قَدْرِ طَاقَتِي وَأَقُولُ فِي مَحْبُوبَتِي شَيْأً
sentences.tr: wa-anā al-ākharu lā-budda-annī abdhulu al-jahda ʿalā qadri ṭāqatī wa-aqūlu fī maḥbūbatī shayʾan
sentences.l: and-I the-other, no escape that-I expend the-effort according-to (the) measure (of) my-strength, and-I-say about my-beloved something.
sentences.i: I too must do my utmost, as far as my strength allows, and say something of my beloved.”
sentences.n: wa-anā al-ākhar, literally “and I the other”, is the colloquial “and I too, I as well”. لابداني is set solid in the print: lā budda, “there is no escape”, and annī, “that I”, run together as one word, and it is pointed here across the joins; lā budda anna is “it must be that”. ʿalā qadri, “according to the measure of”. شيأ is the edition's spelling of shayʾan, “something”, with the hamza on an alif seat (Classical شيئا); the أ is printed, as are the آ of الآخر and the fatha of الجهدَ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ دَهْنَشَ قَامَ إِلَي الصَّبِيَّةِ بُدُورَ وَقَبَّلَهَا بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهَا وَنَظَرَ إِلَى مَيْمُونَةَ وَإِلَى مَعْشُوقَتِهِ بُدُورَ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْقَصِيدَةَ وَهُوَ بِلَاشُعُورٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Dahnasha qāma ilā al-ṣabiyyati Budūra wa-qabbalahā bayna ʿaynayhā wa-naẓara ilā Maymūnata wa-ilā maʿshūqatihi Budūra wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-qaṣīdata wa-huwa bi-lā-shuʿūrin
sentences.l: Then indeed Dahnash rose to the-girl Budūr and-kissed-her between her-two-eyes, and-looked at Maymūna and-at his-beloved Budūr, and-recited, saying, this the-ode, and-he (was) without-awareness:
sentences.i: Then Dahnash went over to the girl Budūr and kissed her between the eyes; he looked at Maymūna and at his beloved Budūr, and, quite carried away, recited this ode:
sentences.n: qāma ilā, “rose (and went) to”. The first الي is printed with a final ي in place of ى; it is still ilā, “to”. ṣabiyya, “girl, young woman”. The shadda of وقبّلها is the print's own. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, as Maymūna did before him. wa-huwa, “and he (was)”, brings in a circumstantial clause on the state of the subject. بلاشعور is set solid in the print: bi-, “with”, + lā, “no”, + shuʿūr, “awareness”, that is “without knowing what he did”, beside himself.

sentences.t:
لَامُوا عَلَى حُبِّ الْمَلِيحِ وَعَنَّفُوا * مَا انْصَفُوا مِنْ جَهْلِهِمْ مَا انْصَفُوا
جُوْدِيْ بِوَصْلِكِ لِلْمُتَيَّمِ اَنَّهُ * اِنْ ذَاقَ هَجْرُكَ بِالتَّخَلُّفِ يَتْلَفُ
وَلَقَدْ بُلِيتُ صَبَابَةً بِمَدَامِعِي * تَحْكِى الدِّمَا مِنْ جَفْنِ عَيْنِي تَذْرُفُ
لَيْسَ الْعَجِيبُ بِمَا اُلَاقِي فِى الْهَوَى * وَعَجِبْتُ جِسْمِي بَعْدَ بُعْدِكَ يُعْرَفُ
حُرِمْتُ وَصْلَكِ اِنْ هَمَمْتُ بِرِيبَةٍ * اَوْ مَلَّ قَلْبِى الْحُبَّ اَوْ يَتَكَلَّفُ
sentences.tr:
lāmū ʿalā ḥubbi al-malīḥi wa-ʿannafū * mā anṣafū min jahlihim mā anṣafū
jūdī bi-waṣliki li-al-mutayyami annahu * in dhāqa hajruka bi-al-takhallufi yatlafu
wa-laqad bulītu ṣabābatan bi-madāmiʿī * taḥkī al-dimā min jafni ʿaynī tadhrufu
laysa al-ʿajību bi-mā ulāqī fī al-hawā * wa-ʿajibtu jismī baʿda buʿdika yuʿrafu
ḥurimtu waṣlaki in hamamtu bi-rībatin * aw malla qalbī al-ḥubba aw yatakallafu
sentences.l:
They-blamed (me) over love (of) the-comely-one, and-they-chided; * not they-were-fair, from their-ignorance, not they-were-fair.
Be-generous with-your(f.)-union to-the-love-enslaved; for-he, * if tastes your-desertion by-the-staying-away, perishes.
And-indeed I-have-been-afflicted (with) passion, with-my-tears * (that) resemble the-blood, from (the) lid (of) my-eye shedding.
Not (is) the-wonder in-what I-meet in the-love; * and-I-marvelled (that) my-body, after your-farness, is-known.
May-I-be-denied your(f.)-union if I-intended a-suspect-thing, * or wearied my-heart (of) the-love, or (if) it-feigns.
sentences.i:
They blamed me for loving the fair one, and chided me; they were unjust in their ignorance, unjust indeed.
Be generous with your union to one enslaved by love; for if he tastes your desertion, your keeping away, he will perish.
I am stricken with passion, and with tears like blood that stream from my eyelids.
The wonder is not in what I suffer in love; what I marvel at is that my body can still be known, now that you are far.
May I be denied union with you if I ever meant anything base, or if my heart tires of love, or merely feigns it.
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -fu. The pointing is the print's own. Line 1: ʿannafa, “to chide harshly”; al-malīḥ, “the comely one”, is masculine, as the beloved usually is in Arabic love poetry. The print points انصفوا with no hamza on the alif; read anṣafū, Form IV, “they dealt fairly”, as the metre requires. min, “from”, gives the cause. Line 2: jūdī, feminine imperative of jāda bi-, “to bestow generously”: the bi- marks the gift; li- marks the one it goes to. mutayyam, “enslaved by love”. The print points اَنّه as annahu; the sense wants innahu, “for he”, and the print's vowel is kept. It also points هَجْرُكَ in the nominative and with a masculine -ka, where the line, speaking to a woman (jūdī, waṣliki), wants the object hajraki, “your desertion”; read it so in sense, but the print's marks are kept. The poem moves between feminine and masculine address again in lines 4 and 5 (buʿdika, waṣlaki): love poetry often speaks to the beloved in the masculine, whoever is meant. yatlafu, “he perishes”, answers in, “if”: after a perfect in the condition (dhāqa), the answer may stand in the indicative, so the -u is regular as well as the rhyme. Line 3: bulītu, passive, “I have been afflicted”; ṣabāba, “ardent love”. bi-, “with”, marks what he is stricken with: his tears. تحكى is spelt with ى for final ي (taḥkī, “they resemble”), as are فى and قلبى below. al-dimā is al-dimāʾ, “blood” (plural of dam), without its hamza, a licence of verse. Line 4: laysa takes bi- on its predicate: “the wonder is not what I meet”. ʿajibtu, “I marvelled”, is followed directly by its clause, with no an or min, which makes the line hard; the sense is that his body is so wasted that it is a wonder anyone still knows it. baʿda buʿdika, “after your being far”, is a play on two words with the same letters. Line 5: ḥurimtu, a perfect used as a curse upon oneself: “may I be denied”. hamma bi-, “to have a mind to”: the verb takes bi- for what is intended. rība, “suspicion”, here something shameful. malla, “to grow weary of”, takes its object directly: al-ḥubba. yatakallafu, “forces itself, feigns”.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And-(the)-saying (of) the-other:
sentences.i: And the words of another poet:
sentences.n: wa-qawlu al-ākhari, “and the saying of the other”, is a heading rather than a sentence: a second poem follows, as by another poet. The آ of الآخر is printed.

sentences.t:
اَقْوَتْ مَعَاهِدُهُمْ بِشَطِّ الْوَادِي * فَبَقِيتُ مَقْتُولاً وَشَطَّ الْوَادِي
وَسَكِرْتُ مِنْ خَمْرِ الْغَرَامِ وَرَقَّصَتْ * عَيْنُ الدُّمُوعِ عَلَى غِنَاءِ الْحَادِي
اَسْعَى لِاَسْعَدَ بِالْوِصَالِ وَحَقَّ لِي * اِنَّ السَّعَادَةَ فِي بُدُورِ سُعَادِ
لَمْ اَدْرِ مِنْ اَيِّ الثَّلٰثَةِ اَشْتَكِي * وَلَقَدْ عَدَدْتُ فَاَصْغِ لِلْاِعْدَادِ
مِنْ لَحْظِهَا السَّيَّافِ اَمْ مِنْ قَدِّهَا الرَّمَّاحِ اَمْ مِنْ صُدْغِهَا الزَّرَّادِ
قَالَتْ وَقَدْ فَتَّشْتُ عَنْهَا كُلَّ مَنْ * لَاقَيْتُهُ مِنْ حَاضِرٍ اَوْ بَادِيْ
اَنَا فِيْ فُؤَادِكَ فَارْمِ طَرْفَكَ نَحْوَهُ * تَرْنِيْ فَقُلْتُ لَهَا وَاَيْنَ فُؤَادِيْ
sentences.tr:
aqwat maʿāhiduhum bi-shaṭṭi al-wādī * fa-baqītu maqtūlan wa-shaṭṭa al-wādī
wa-sakirtu min khamri al-gharāmi wa-raqqaṣat * ʿaynu al-dumūʿi ʿalā ghināʾi al-ḥādī
asʿā li-asʿada bi-al-wiṣāli wa-ḥaqqa lī * inna al-saʿādata fī budūri Suʿādi
lam adri min ayyi al-thalāthati ashtakī * wa-laqad ʿadadtu fa-aṣghi li-al-iʿdādi
min laḥẓihā al-sayyāfi am min qaddihā al-rammāḥi am min ṣudghihā al-zarrādi
qālat wa-qad fattashtu ʿanhā kulla man * lāqaytuhu min ḥāḍirin aw bādī
anā fī fuʾādika fa-irmi ṭarfaka naḥwahu * tarnī fa-qultu lahā wa-ayna fuʾādī
sentences.l:
Became-empty their-haunts at-(the)-bank (of) the-valley; * so-I-remained slain, and-went-far the-valley.
And-I-grew-drunk from (the) wine (of) the-passion, and-set-dancing * (the) eye (of) the-tears to (the) singing (of) the-camel-driver.
I-strive in-order-that-I-be-happy with-the-union, and-(it is)-due to-me: * indeed the-happiness (is) in (the) full-moons (of) Suʿād.
Not I-know from which (of) the-three I-complain; * and-indeed I-have-counted, so-lend-ear to-the-count:
From her-glance, the-swordsman, or from her-stature, the-lancer, or from her-temple-lock, the-mail-maker?
She-said, and-already I-had-searched for-her (among) everyone whom * I-met, of settled-one or desert-one:
I (am) in your-heart, so-cast your-glance toward-it, * you-will-see-me. So-I-said to-her: And-where (is) my-heart?
sentences.i:
Their old haunts lie empty on the valley's bank, and I am left slain, for the valley has gone far away.
I grew drunk on the wine of passion, and the spring of my tears was set dancing to the camel-driver's song.
I strive to win happiness through union, and it is my right: for happiness lies in the full moons of Suʿād.
I cannot tell which of the three to complain of; I have counted them, so listen to the count:
Is it her glance, the swordsman, or her figure, the lancer, or her temple-curl, the maker of mail?
She said (and I had searched for her among everyone I met, of town or desert):
“I am in your heart: cast your eye toward it and you will see me.” And I said to her, “And where is my heart?”
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -ādī. The pointing is the print's own. Line 1 opens as the classical ode opens, on the deserted camp-site of the beloved's people. aqwā, Form IV, “to become empty of people”; maʿāhid, “haunts, places one knew”. The line ends on the same two words in two senses: bi-shaṭṭi al-wādī, “at the bank of the valley” (bi-, “at”), and wa-shaṭṭa al-wādī, “and the valley has gone far”, from shaṭṭa, “to be distant”: the place of the beloved is out of reach. Line 2: ʿayn is both “eye” and “spring of water”, and the ʿayn of tears is both at once. raqqaṣa, Form II, is “to make dance”; the print gives it no object, so the sense is that the eye's spring is set leaping in time with the ḥādī, the driver who sings to urge the camels on — here the caravan that carries the beloved away. ʿalā, “on, to”, marks the music danced to. Line 3: li-, “so that”, with the subjunctive asʿada, “that I may be happy”; asʿā, asʿada, al-saʿāda and Suʿād all sound the letters s and ʿ. budūr, “full moons”, plural of badr, is also the princess's name: the happiness lies in Budūr. Suʿād is the stock name of the beloved in Arabic love poetry; it would normally be Suʿāda, and the -i is the rhyme. wa-ḥaqqa lī, “and it is due to me”: ḥaqqa, “to be rightful”, with li- for the one it is due to. Line 4: lam adri, from darā, “to know”: “I do not know”. الثلٰثة, al-thalātha, “the three”, is spelt without the long alif and printed with the dagger alif. aṣghi, imperative of aṣghā, “to lend an ear”; li- marks what is listened to. iʿdād is properly “making ready”; here it stands for the count just made (ʿadadtu, “I have counted”), for the sake of the rhyme. Line 5 is printed whole, without the * that divides the halves. Each of the three is given a trade in the intensive form faʿʿāl: the glance is a sayyāf, “swordsman”, the straight figure (qadd) a rammāḥ, “lancer”, and the ṣudgh, the temple and the curl of hair lying on it, a zarrād, “maker of chain mail”, since ringlets were likened to the links of mail. Line 6: wa-qad with the perfect sets a circumstance: “when I had already searched”. fattasha ʿan, “to search for”: ʿan marks the one sought. min, “of”, gives the kinds: ḥāḍir, the settled townsman, and bādī (Classical bādin), the desert nomad, a pair meaning “everyone”. Line 7: irmi, imperative of ramā, “to cast”; ṭarf, “glance, eye”. تَرْنِيْ is the print's pointing of “you will see me”, the jussive of raʾā answering the imperative; the regular form is taranī, and the print's tarnī fits the metre. The ؤ of فؤاد, “heart”, is printed. Her answer is the lover's trap: she is in his heart, but she has taken his heart, so it is nowhere to be found.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ مِنْ دَهْنَشَ هٰذَا الشِّعْرَ قَالَتْ لَهُ أَحْسَنْتَ يَادَهْنَشُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Maymūnatu min Dahnasha hādhā al-shiʿra qālat lahu aḥsanta yā-Dahnashu
sentences.l: So-when heard Maymūna from Dahnash this the-poetry, she-said to-him: You-have-done-well, O-Dahnash!
sentences.i: When Maymūna heard these verses from Dahnash, she said to him, “Well done, Dahnash!
sentences.n: aḥsanta, “you have done well”, Form IV of ḥasuna, is the stock praise for a poem well made. يادهنش, yā Dahnashu, “O Dahnash”, is set solid in the print, the vocative yā joined to the name, and is pointed here as one word. Dahnash, a foreign name, is a diptote: min Dahnasha, with no kasra or tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ أَيُّ هٰذَيْنِ الِاثْنَيْنِ أَحْسَنُ فَقَالَ لَهَا مَحْبُوبَتِي بُدُورُ أَحْسَنُ مِنْ مَحْبُوبِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin ayyu hādhayni al-ithnayni aḥsanu fa-qāla lahā maḥbūbatī Budūru aḥsanu min maḥbūbiki
sentences.l: But which (of) these-two, the-two, (is) fairer? And-he-said to-her: My-beloved Budūr (is) fairer than your-beloved.
sentences.i: But which of these two is the fairer?” He said to her, “My beloved Budūr is fairer than yours.”
sentences.n: ayy, “which?”, takes the pair it chooses between in the genitive: ayyu hādhayni, “which of these two”; its shadda is the print's own. al-ithnayni, “the two”, stands in apposition to hādhayni. aḥsan is the elative of ḥasan, “beautiful, good”; with min it compares: aḥsanu min, “fairer than”. Budūr is a diptote and takes no tanwīn.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَيْمُونَةُ كَذَبْتَ يَا مَلْعُونُ بَلْ مَحْبُوبِي أَحْسَنُ مِنْ مَعْشُوقَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Maymūnatu kadhabta yā malʿūnu bal maḥbūbī aḥsanu min maʿshūqatika
sentences.l: And-said to-him Maymūna: You-have-lied, O accursed-one! Rather my-beloved (is) fairer than your-beloved(-woman).
sentences.i: Maymūna said to him, “You lie, you accursed wretch! No: my beloved is fairer than your sweetheart.”
sentences.n: kadhabta, “you have lied”: the perfect, for a lie just told, where English says “you lie”. bal, “nay, rather”, sets the true claim against the false. maʿshūqa, “beloved (woman)”, is the passive participle of ʿashiqa, “to love passionately”; the two quarrellers use maḥbūb and maʿshūq as synonyms.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ دَهْنَشُ مَعْشُوقَتِي أَحْسَنُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Dahnashu maʿshūqatī aḥsanu
sentences.l: And-said Dahnash: My-beloved (is) fairer.
sentences.i: Dahnash said, “My sweetheart is the fairer.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا لَمْ يَزَالَا يُعَارِضَانِ مَعَ بَعْضِهِمَا فِى الْكَلَامِ حَتَّى صَرَخَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ عَلَى دَهْنَشَ وَأَرَادَتْ أَنْ تَبْطِشَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā lam yazālā yuʿāriḍāni maʿa baʿḍihimā fī al-kalāmi ḥattā ṣarakhat Maymūnatu ʿalā Dahnasha wa-arādat an tabṭisha bihi
sentences.l: Then indeed-they-two not ceased contradicting with each-other in the-talk, until shouted Maymūna at Dahnash, and-she-wanted to fall-upon him.
sentences.i: So the two went on contradicting each other until Maymūna screamed at Dahnash and made to fall upon him.
sentences.n: lam yazālā yuʿāriḍāni, “they did not cease contradicting”: zāla with a negative means “to go on”, and the imperfect after it says what they went on doing. ʿāraḍa, Form III, “to oppose, contradict”, already implies a second party; maʿa baʿḍihimā, “with each other”, says it again, a spoken habit the Nights often has. ṣarakha ʿalā, “to shout at”. baṭasha bi-, “to seize violently, attack”: the verb takes bi- for its victim. an takes the subjunctive: an tabṭisha.

sentences.t: فَذَلَّ لَهَا وَرَقَّقَ كَلَامَهُ وَقَالَ لَهَا لَا يَصْعُبْ عَلَيْكِ الْحَقُّ فَأَبْطِلِي قَوْلَكِ وَقَوْلِي فَإِنَّ كُلًّا مِنَّا يَشْهَدُ لِمَعْشُوقِهِ أَنَّهُ أَحْسَنُ
sentences.tr: fa-dhalla lahā wa-raqqaqa kalāmahu wa-qāla lahā lā yaṣʿub ʿalayki al-ḥaqqu fa-abṭilī qawlaki wa-qawlī fa-inna kullan minnā yashhadu li-maʿshūqihi annahu aḥsanu
sentences.l: So-he-was-humbled to-her and-softened his-speech and-said to-her: Let-not be-hard on-you the-truth; so-annul your-word and-my-word, for each of-us bears-witness for-his-beloved that he (is) fairer.
sentences.i: At that he humbled himself before her and softened his words, and said to her, “Do not let the truth weigh on you. Set aside what you say and what I say, for each of us bears witness for his own beloved that he is the fairer.
sentences.n: dhalla li-, “to humble oneself before”; raqqaqa, Form II, “to make soft, gentle”: both shaddas are the print's own. lā yaṣʿub is a prohibition in the third person: “let not the truth be hard”. abṭala, Form IV, “to annul, set aside”; abṭilī is its feminine imperative. kullan minnā, “each one of us”: kull in the accusative after inna; the shaddas of كلّا and منّا are printed. li-maʿshūqihi, “for his beloved”: li- marks the one the testimony favours; the masculine is generic, “each for his own”.

sentences.t: فَيُعْرِضُ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنَّا عَنْ كَلَامِهِ وَنَطْلُبُ مَنْ يَفْصِلُ الْحُكْمَ بَيْنَنَا وَنَعْتَمِدُ عَلَى مَا يَقُولُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-yuʿriḍu kullu wāḥidin minnā ʿan kalāmihi wa-naṭlubu man yafṣilu al-ḥukma baynanā wa-naʿtamidu ʿalā mā yaqūluhu
sentences.l: So-turns-away each one of-us from his-speech, and-we-seek (one) who decides the-judgement between-us, and-we-rely on what he-says-it.
sentences.i: So let each of us draw back from his claim, and let us look for someone to settle the judgement between us, and abide by whatever he says.”
sentences.n: The plain imperfects here propose rather than state: “let each … let us”. aʿraḍa ʿan, Form IV, “to turn away from, give up”. man, “one who”, stands without an antecedent: “someone who”. faṣala al-ḥukma, “to decide the judgement, settle the case”. iʿtamada ʿalā, Form VIII, “to rely on”. mā yaqūluhu, “what he says”: the -hu points back to mā; the shadda of منّا is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَيْمُونَةُ رَضِيتُ بِذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Maymūnatu raḍītu bi-dhālika
sentences.l: And-said to-him Maymūna: I-am-content with-that.
sentences.i: Maymūna said to him, “I agree to that.”
sentences.n: raḍiya bi-, “to be content with, accept”: the verb takes bi- for what is accepted.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَقَّتْ بِكَفِّهَا الْأَرْضَ فَطَلَعَ مِنْهَا عِفْرِيتٌ أَعْوَرُ أَحْدَبُ أَجْرَبُ
sentences.tr: thumma daqqat bi-kaffihā al-arḍa fa-ṭalaʿa minhā ʿifrītun aʿwaru aḥdabu ajrabu
sentences.l: Then she-struck with-her-palm the-earth, and-came-up from-it an-ifrit, one-eyed, hunchbacked, mangy.
sentences.i: Then she struck the ground with the flat of her hand, and up out of it came an ifrit, one-eyed, hunchbacked and scabby.
sentences.n: daqqa, “to knock, strike”: bi- marks the hand she strikes with, kaff, “palm”. ṭalaʿa min, “to come up out of”. aʿwar, aḥdab, ajrab, “one-eyed, hunchbacked, mangy”: the afʿal pattern names bodily defects, and these adjectives are diptotes, so they take no tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَعَيْنَاةُ مَشْقُوقَتَانِ فِي وَجْهِهِ بِالطُّولِ وَفِي رَأْسِهِ سَبْعَةُ قُرُونٍ وَلَهُ أَرْبَعُ ذَوَائِبَ مِنَ الشَّعْرِ مُسْتَرْسِلَةٌ إِلَى كَعْبَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿaynāhu mashqūqatāni fī wajhihi bi-al-ṭūli wa-fī raʾsihi sabʿatu qurūnin wa-lahu arbaʿu dhawāʾiba mina al-shaʿri mustarsilatun ilā kaʿbayhi
sentences.l: And-his-two-eyes (were) split in his-face along-the-length, and-in his-head (were) seven horns, and-to-him (were) four locks of the-hair hanging-loose to his-two-ankles.
sentences.i: His two eyes were slit lengthwise in his face, there were seven horns on his head, and he had four locks of hair hanging loose down to his ankles.
sentences.n: عيناة, ʿaynāhu, “his two eyes”, writes the pronoun -hu with ة, a habit of this print; يداة and رجلاة below are the same. (He is called one-eyed and has two eyes: the tale does not stop over it.) bi-al-ṭūl, “lengthwise”: bi- gives the manner. sabʿatu qurūnin: the numbers three to ten take the opposite gender to the singular of the thing counted (qarn, “horn”, is masculine, so sabʿa) and a genitive plural after them. dhuʾāba, pl. dhawāʾib, “a lock, a braid of hair”, is a diptote, so the genitive ends in -a; the ئ is printed, and so is the ء of رأسه. mustarsila, “hanging loose”, is feminine singular, as a plural of things takes. kaʿb, “ankle”; kaʿbayhi, “his two ankles”.

sentences.t: وَيَدَاةُ مِثْلُ الْمَدَارِي وَرِجْلَاةُ مِثْلُ الصَّوَارِي وَلَهُ أَظْفَارٌ مِثْلُ أَظْفَارِ الْأَسَدِ وَحَوَافِرُ مِثْلُ حَوَافِرِ الْحِمَارِ الْوَحْشِيِّ
sentences.tr: wa-yadāhu mithlu al-madārī wa-rijlāhu mithlu al-ṣawārī wa-lahu aẓfārun mithlu aẓfāri al-asadi wa-ḥawāfiru mithlu ḥawāfiri al-ḥimāri al-waḥshiyyi
sentences.l: And-his-two-hands (were) like the-pitchforks, and-his-two-legs like the-masts, and-to-him (were) claws like (the) claws (of) the-lion, and-hooves like (the) hooves (of) the-ass, the-wild.
sentences.i: His hands were like pitchforks and his legs like ships' masts; he had claws like a lion's claws and hooves like the hooves of the wild ass.
sentences.n: The rhyme pairs al-madārī with al-ṣawārī. madārī is the plural of midrā (also midrāt), in the old lexicons a long-toothed comb or pin of iron or wood, and in later Egyptian speech a wooden winnowing fork; prongs suit hands with long spread fingers, but the exact picture is not certain. ṣawārī is the plural of ṣārī, “mast”. rijl is properly “foot”, but here the whole leg. ẓufr, pl. aẓfār, “nail, claw”; ḥāfir, pl. ḥawāfir, “hoof”, a diptote, hence no tanwīn. al-ḥimār al-waḥshī, “the wild ass”, is the onager.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا طَلَعَ ذٰلِكَ الْعِفْرِيتُ وَرَأَى مَيْمُونَةَ قَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَوَقَفَ مُكَتَّفًا وَقَالَ لَهَا مَا حَاجَتُكِ أَيُّهَا السَّيِّدَةُ يَا بِنْتَ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṭalaʿa dhālika al-ʿifrītu wa-raʾā Maymūnata qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhā wa-waqafa mukattafan wa-qāla lahā mā ḥājatuki ayyuhā al-sayyidatu yā binta al-maliki
sentences.l: So-when came-up that the-ifrit and-saw Maymūna, he-kissed the-ground between her-two-hands and-stood with-arms-folded, and-said to-her: What (is) your-need, O the-lady, O daughter (of) the-king?
sentences.i: When the ifrit had come up and saw Maymūna, he kissed the ground before her and stood with his arms folded, and said to her, “What is your need, my lady, daughter of the king?”
sentences.n: qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhā, “he kissed the ground between her hands”, that is, before her: the obeisance of a servant to his sovereign; the shadda of قبّل is the print's. The ء of رأى is printed. mukattaf, “with arms bound”, here folded across the chest, the posture of one waiting on orders. The kasra of حاجتكِ is printed, to show that a woman is addressed. ayyuhā, the masculine form, is used for a woman here, where Classical Arabic would have ayyatuhā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَاقَشْقَشُ إِنِّي أُرِيدُأَنْ تَحْكُمَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ هٰذَا الْمَلْعُونِ دَهْنَشَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā-Qashqashu innī urīdu-an taḥkuma baynī wa-bayna hādhā al-malʿūni Dahnasha
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: O-Qashqash, indeed-I want-that you-judge between-me and-between this the-accursed, Dahnash.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Qashqash, I want you to judge between me and this accursed Dahnash.”
sentences.n: ياقشقش, yā Qashqashu, “O Qashqash”, and اريدان, urīdu an, “I want that”, are each set solid in the print and are pointed here as one word apiece. an takes the subjunctive: an taḥkuma. ḥakama bayna … wa-bayna, “to judge between … and”: Arabic repeats bayna before each party. Dahnash stands in apposition to al-malʿūn and shares its genitive, without tanwīn: Dahnasha.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا حَكَتْ لَهُ عَلَى الْقِصَّةِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهَا إِلَى آخِرِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahā ḥakat lahu ʿalā al-qiṣṣati min awwalihā ilā ākhirihā
sentences.l: Then indeed-she told to-him about the-story from its-first to its-last.
sentences.i: Then she told him the whole story from beginning to end.
sentences.n: ḥakā, “to relate”, takes the tale as its direct object in Classical Arabic; ḥakā ʿalā, “to tell of”, is the spoken usage the Nights often has. The آ of آخرها is printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَهَا نَظَرَ الْعِفْرِيتُ قَشْقَشُ إِلَى وَجْهِ ذٰلِكَ الصَّبِيِّ وَوَجْهِ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ فَرَآهُمَا مُتَعَانِقَيْنِ وَهُمَا نَائِمَانِ وَمِعْصَمُ كُلٍّ مِنْهُمَا تَحْتَ عُنُقِ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿindahā naẓara al-ʿifrītu Qashqashu ilā wajhi dhālika al-ṣabiyyi wa-wajhi tilka al-ṣabiyyati fa-raʾāhumā mutaʿāniqayni wa-humā nāʾimāni wa-miʿṣamu kullin minhumā taḥta ʿunuqi al-ākhari
sentences.l: So-at-it looked the-ifrit Qashqash at (the) face (of) that the-youth and-(the)-face (of) that the-maiden, and-he-saw-them-two embracing-each-other, and-they-two (were) sleeping, and-(the)-wrist (of) each of-them-two (was) under (the) neck (of) the-other.
sentences.i: At that the ifrit Qashqash looked at the face of the youth and the face of the girl, and saw them lying asleep in each other's arms, the wrist of each beneath the other's neck.
sentences.n: fa-ʿindahā, “and thereupon”, literally “and at it”, is one of the narrator's hinges. mutaʿāniqayni, Form VI, “embracing one another”, is accusative as the state (ḥāl) of the object -humā. wa-humā nāʾimāni, “they being asleep”: a circumstantial clause brought in by wa-. miʿṣam, “wrist”. The hamza and madda of رآهما, نائمان and الآخر are printed.

sentences.t: وَهُمَا فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ مُتَشَابِهَانِ وَفِى الْمَلَاحَةِ مُتَسَاوِيَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-humā fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli mutashābihāni wa-fī al-malāḥati mutasāwiyāni
sentences.l: And-they-two (were) in the-beauty and-the-loveliness resembling-each-other, and-in the-grace equal-to-each-other.
sentences.i: In beauty and loveliness they were alike, and in grace they were equal.
sentences.n: The rhyme falls on two duals, mutashābihāni and mutasāwiyāni, both Form VI, the form of mutual action: “resembling each other”, “equal to each other”. ḥusn, jamāl and malāḥa are near-synonyms for beauty; malāḥa, from milḥ, “salt”, is the piquant charm of a face.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الْمَارِدُ قَشْقَشُ إِلَيْهِمَا وَتَعَجَّبَ مِنْ حُسْنِهِمَا وَجَمَا لِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara al-māridu Qashqashu ilayhimā wa-taʿajjaba min ḥusnihimā wa-jamālihimā
sentences.l: And-looked the-rebel-jinni Qashqash at-them-two and-marvelled at their-beauty and-their-loveliness,
sentences.i: The marid Qashqash gazed at them, wondering at their beauty and their loveliness,
sentences.n: al-mārid, “the rebellious one”, is another name for a jinni of the strong, defiant sort; the narrator uses it for Qashqash as a synonym of ʿifrīt. وجما لهما, wa-jamālihimā, “and their loveliness”, is broken by a space in the print, which is kept; it is one word, jamāl with -himā, “of the two of them”, and is pointed as one. taʿajjaba min, “to wonder at”.

sentences.t: وَالْتَفَتَ إِلَى مَيْمُونَةَ وَدَهْنَشَ بَعْدَ أَنْ أَطَالَ إِلَى الصَّبِيِّ وَالصَّبِيَّةِ الِالْتِفَاتَ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-iltafata ilā Maymūnata wa-Dahnasha baʿda an aṭāla ilā al-ṣabiyyi wa-al-ṣabiyyati al-iltifāta wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: and-he-turned to Maymūna and-Dahnash, after that he-had-made-long toward the-youth and-the-maiden the-turning(-to-look), and-he-recited, saying, these the-verses:
sentences.i: and, when he had looked long upon the youth and the girl, he turned to Maymūna and Dahnash and recited these verses:
sentences.n: aṭāla al-iltifāta ilā, “to make long the looking toward”: the verbal noun iltifāt, from iltafata, “to turn (to look)”, is the object of aṭāla, and the phrase ilā al-ṣabiyyi wa-al-ṣabiyyati stands between verb and object. The same verb, iltafata, has just served for turning to Maymūna and Dahnash. baʿda an with the perfect, “after he had”. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”. bayt, pl. abyāt, is a line of verse.

sentences.t:
زُرْ مَنْ تُحِبُّ وَدَعْ مَقَالَةَ حَاسِدِ * لَيْسَ الْحَسُوْدُ عَلَى الْهَوَى بِمُسَاعِدِ
لَنْ يَخْلُقَ الرَّحْمٰنُ اَحْسَنَ مَنْظَرًا * مِنْ عَاشِقَيْنِ عَلَى فِرَاشٍ وَاحِدِ
مُتَعَانِقَيْنِ عَلَيْهِمَا حُلَلُ الرِّضَى * مُتَوَسِّدَيْنِ بِمِعْصَمٍ وَبِسَاعِدِ
وَاِذَا صَفَالَكَ مِنْ زَمَانِكَ وَاحِدٌ * فَهُوَ الْمُرَادُ وَعِشْ بِذَاكَ الْوَاحِدِ
وَاِذَا تَاَلَّفَتِ الْقُلُوْبُ عَلَى الْهَوَى * فَالنَّاسُ تَضْرِبُ فِي حَدِيْدٍ بَارِدِ
يَا مَنْ يَلُوْمُ عَلَى الْهَوَى اَهْلَ الْهَوَى * هَلْ تَسْتَطِيْعُ صَلَاحَ قَلْبٍ فَاسِدِ
يَارَبِّ يَا رَحْمٰنُ تَجْمَعُ بَيْنَنَا * قَبْلَ الْمَمَاتِ وَلَوْ بِيَوْمٍ وَاحِدِ
sentences.tr:
zur man tuḥibbu wa-daʿ maqālata ḥāsidi * laysa al-ḥasūdu ʿalā al-hawā bi-musāʿidi
lan yakhluqa al-raḥmānu aḥsana manẓaran * min ʿāshiqayni ʿalā firāshin wāḥidi
mutaʿāniqayni ʿalayhimā ḥulalu al-riḍā * mutawassidayni bi-miʿṣamin wa-bi-sāʿidi
wa-idhā ṣafā-laka min zamānika wāḥidun * fa-huwa al-murādu wa-ʿish bi-dhāka al-wāḥidi
wa-idhā taʾallafati al-qulūbu ʿalā al-hawā * fa-al-nāsu taḍribu fī ḥadīdin bāridi
yā man yalūmu ʿalā al-hawā ahla al-hawā * hal tastaṭīʿu ṣalāḥa qalbin fāsidi
yā-rabbi yā raḥmānu tajmaʿu baynanā * qabla al-mamāti wa-law bi-yawmin wāḥidi
sentences.l:
Visit whom you-love, and-leave (the) talk (of) an-envier: * not (is) the-envious-one in the-love a-helper.
Never will-create the-Merciful a-fairer sight * than two-lovers on a-bed single,
embracing-each-other, upon-them-two (the) robes (of) the-contentment, * pillowing-themselves on-a-wrist and-on-a-forearm.
And-when is-pure for-you from your-time one, * then-he (is) the-desired: and-live by-that the-one.
And-when join-together the-hearts in the-love, * then-the-people strike on iron cold.
O (you) who blames for the-love (the) people (of) the-love, * can you (bring about the) mending (of) a-heart corrupt?
O-my-Lord, O Merciful-one, you-gather between-us * before the-death, even-if for-a-day single.
sentences.i:
Visit the one you love, and leave the envier to talk: the envious are no helpers in love.
The Merciful will never create a fairer sight than two lovers on a single bed,
in each other's arms, robed in the garments of content, pillowed on a wrist and a forearm.
When time grants you one who is true to you, that one is all you could wish: live for that one alone.
When hearts are joined together in love, the world is beating on cold iron.
You who blame the people of love for loving, can you set right a heart gone astray?
My Lord, O Merciful, bring us together before death, if only for a single day.
sentences.n: The print has فالمّاس, a misprint for فالنّاس, corrected here: its shadda after the article is the doubling only a “sun” letter such as n takes, and al-mās, “diamond”, fits neither that pointing nor the sense. Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -idi. The pointing is otherwise the print's own. Line 1: maqāla, “talk, what is said”; ʿalā al-hawā, “in the matter of love”; the bi- of bi-musāʿidi only strengthens the predicate of laysa: “no helper at all”. Line 2: lan with the subjunctive, “will never”, denies the future. Line 3: the duals carry on from ʿāshiqayni, describing the pair as Qashqash sees them. ḥulal is the plural of ḥulla, a robe, a suit of fine clothes; al-riḍā, “contentment”, printed with ى. mutawassid, Form V, “taking as a pillow”, with bi- for the pillow; sāʿid, “forearm”. Line 4: صفالك, ṣafā laka, “is clear, true to you”, is set solid in the print and is pointed as one word. Line 5: to beat cold iron is to labour in vain: once hearts are joined, whoever tries to part them wastes his strokes. taḍribu is feminine, as a word for a mass of people may be. Line 6: ahl al-hawā, “the people of love”, lovers. Line 7: يارب, yā rabbi, “O my Lord”, is set solid. tajmaʿu, “you gather”, is a plain imperfect where a prayer would use the imperative; it reads as a wish: “may you bring us together”. wa-law, “even if (only)”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ قَشْقَشَ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى مَيْمُونَةَ وَدَهْنَشَ وَقَالَ لَهُمَا وَاللّٰهِ إِنْ أَرَدْتُمَا الْحَقَّ فَإِنِّي أَقُولُ إِنَّ الِا ثْنَيْنِ سَوَاءٌ فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ وَالْبَهْجَةِ وَالْكَمَالِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿifrīta Qashqasha iltafata ilā Maymūnata wa-Dahnasha wa-qāla lahumā wa-Allāhi in aradtumā al-ḥaqqa fa-innī aqūlu inna al-ithnayni sawāʾun fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli wa-al-bahjati wa-al-kamāli
sentences.l: Then indeed the-ifrit Qashqash turned to Maymūna and-Dahnash and-said to-them-two: By-God, if you-two-want the-truth, then-indeed-I say that the-two (are) equal in the-beauty and-the-loveliness, and-the-radiance and-the-perfection,
sentences.i: Then the ifrit Qashqash turned to Maymūna and Dahnash and said to them, “By God, if you want the truth, I say that the two are equal in beauty and loveliness, in radiance and perfection,
sentences.n: After inna, Qashqash shares the accusative of al-ʿifrīt: al-ʿifrīta Qashqasha. lahumā and aradtumā are duals: he speaks to the pair. aqūlu inna: after qāla and its forms, “that” is inna, not anna. الا ثنين, al-ithnayni, “the two”, is broken by a space in the print, which is kept; it is pointed as one word. sawāʾ, “equal, alike”, is a noun and stays singular for two. The rhyme pairs al-jamāl with al-kamāl.

sentences.t: وَلَا يُفَرَّقُ بَيْنَهُمَا بِالتَّذْكِيرِ وَالتَّأْنِيثِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā yufarraqu baynahumā bi-al-tadhkīri wa-al-taʾnīthi
sentences.l: and-not is-(it)-distinguished between-them-two by-the-masculine and-the-feminine;
sentences.i: and their being man and woman makes no difference between them.
sentences.n: yufarraqu, the passive of Form II farraqa, “to tell apart”, has no subject: “no distinction is made between them”. bi- gives the ground of the distinction. tadhkīr and taʾnīth, “making masculine” and “making feminine”, are the grammarians' words for gender, used here of the two sleepers: one is male and one female, and that makes neither of them the lovelier.

sentences.t: وَعِنْدِي رَأْيٌ آخَرُ وَهُوَ أَنَّنَا نُنَبِّهُ أَحَدَ هُمَا مِنْ غَيْرِ عِلْمِ الثَّانِي
sentences.tr: wa-ʿindī raʾyun ākharu wa-huwa annanā nunabbihu aḥadahumā min ghayri ʿilmi al-thānī
sentences.l: And-with-me (is) an-opinion other, and-it (is) that-we wake one-of-them-two without (the) knowledge (of) the-second;
sentences.i: But I have another plan: we will wake one of them without the other's knowing,
sentences.n: raʾyun ākharu: ākhar, “other”, is a diptote and takes no tanwīn; its damma is the print's own, as is the ء of رأي. nabbaha, Form II, “to rouse, wake”; the shadda is printed. احد هما, aḥadahumā, “one of the two”, is broken by a space in the print, which is kept; it is pointed as one word. min ghayri ʿilmi, “without the knowledge of”; the vowels of عِلْم are printed. al-thānī, “the second”, here “the other”.

sentences.t: فَكُلُّ مَنِ الْتَهَبَ عَلَى رَفِيقِهِ فَهُوَ دُونَهُ فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-kullu mani iltahaba ʿalā rafīqihi fa-huwa dūnahu fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli
sentences.l: so-every who blazes-up for his-companion, then-he (is) beneath-him in the-beauty and-the-loveliness.
sentences.i: and whichever of them is set aflame with desire for the other is the lesser in beauty and loveliness.”
sentences.n: kullu man, “everyone who”; fa- before huwa brings in the conclusion, as after a condition. iltahaba, Form VIII, “to blaze up”, of passion: ʿalā marks the one desired. dūna, “below, short of”: “he is beneath him in beauty”. The test rests on the idea that the lovelier of the two will not be the one overcome by the other's beauty.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ هٰذَا الرَّأْيُ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat Maymūnatu hādhā al-raʾyu huwa al-ṣawābu
sentences.l: And-said Maymūna: This the-opinion, it (is) the-right.
sentences.i: Maymūna said, “This plan is the right one,”
sentences.n: huwa, “it”, stands between subject and predicate when both are definite, to mark where the sentence divides: “this plan, it is the right thing”. The ء of الرأي is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ دَهْنَشُ رَضِيتُ بِذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla Dahnashu raḍītu bi-dhālika
sentences.l: And-said Dahnash: I-am-content with-that.
sentences.i: and Dahnash said, “I agree to that.”

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ انْقَلَبَ دَهْنَشُ فِي صُورَةِ بُرْغُوثٍ وَقَرَصَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ فَوَثَبَ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ مَرْعُوبًا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika inqalaba Dahnashu fī ṣūrati burghūthin wa-qaraṣa Qamara al-Zamāni fa-wathaba min manāmihi marʿūban
sentences.l: So-at that, turned Dahnash in(to the) form (of) a-flea and-nipped Qamar al-Zamān, and-he-leapt-up from his-sleep terrified.
sentences.i: Thereupon Dahnash changed himself into the shape of a flea and bit Qamar al-Zamān, who started up out of his sleep in terror.
sentences.n: inqalaba, Form VII, “to be turned over, changed”: inqalaba fī ṣūrati, “to turn into the form of”, with fī where ilā is more usual. qaraṣa, “to pinch, nip”, is what a flea does: “to bite”. wathaba, “to leap”; the subject is now Qamar al-Zamān. marʿūb, “frightened”, is accusative as a state (ḥāl).

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
